n: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix

faq.a: High‑risk human papillomavirus infection, especially types 16 and 18.
faq.q: What is the most common cause of cervical SCC?

faq.a: Yes, vaccines covering HPV 16/18 reduce the incidence of SCC by >90% in vaccinated populations.
faq.q: Can HPV vaccination prevent cervical cancer?

faq.a: It localises abnormal areas, guides biopsy, and assesses extent of disease for staging.
faq.q: Why is colposcopy mandatory after an abnormal Pap?

exam: A 38‑year‑old presents with post‑coital bleeding; Pap shows ASCUS. What is the next step? — Perform HPV DNA testing; if positive, proceed to colposcopy.
A patient with stage IB2 SCC is scheduled for surgery. What adjuvant therapy is recommended? — Radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin.
During colposcopy, a lesion shows a ‘punched‑out’ ulcer with a white halo. What does this indicate? — A high‑grade CIN or invasive SCC; biopsy is required.
A woman with SCC has persistent vaginal discharge and fever. What complication should you suspect? — Pelvic abscess or sepsis; urgent imaging and antibiotics.
A patient with SCC refuses radiotherapy. What alternative is acceptable for early stage disease? — Radical trachelectomy if fertility preservation is desired.
A biopsy shows keratin pearls. What is the significance? — Histological hallmark of squamous differentiation, confirming SCC.
ai.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: A common cervical cancer subtype driven by HPV, presenting with post‑coital bleeding or abnormal Pap. Diagnosis relies on cytology, colposcopy and biopsy; management is staged, combining surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

sections.p: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) arises from the ectocervical epithelium. It is the most frequent cervical cancer type, especially where HPV vaccination coverage is low.
SCC follows a predictable natural history: HPV infection → cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) → invasive cancer.

t.b: Screen for abnormal cytology; ASCUS or LSIL may need repeat or colposcopy
Detect high‑risk types; positive in >90% of SCC
Define tumour size and parametrial invasion for staging
Rule out distant metastases in stage III/IV

b: Early symptoms are subtle; education reduces late diagnosis
sections.p: Patients often present with post‑coital bleeding, abnormal discharge or pelvic pain. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation leads to advanced disease.

t.b: Look for cervical mass, friability, bleeding
Assess parametrial involvement; positive for induration or fixation
Detect bulky tumour or ascites when MRI unavailable

sections.p: Examiners probe history, examination, staging, and management choices. Focus on the sequence of investigations and the rationale for treatment modalities.

b: HPV DNA testing improves detection of high‑risk lesions
sections.p: Misinterpreting ASCUS as benign, over‑relying on Pap alone, and neglecting HPV testing. Assuming all cervical cancers are adenocarcinoma.
